cim: Brazilian Army receives 30 quadcopters to develop a drone swarm system
cim_eredeti: Brazilian Army receives 30 quadcopters to develop a drone swarm system
szoveg_eredeti:
The Military Institute of Engineering (IME), through its Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence, Robotics and Cybernetics (LIARC), received the first batch of ten aircraft developed by the Brazilian company SkyDrones. The delivery was announced by the Army itself on 13 November, while LRCA Defense Consulting reported, after consulting the company, that all 30 planned units had already been delivered to the Institute.

The aim of the programme is to develop a system in which a single operator can supervise multiple drones from a ground station, while the aircraft carry out coordinated movements. To that end, LIARC is responsible for developing the artificial intelligence, the coordination algorithms and the integrated control software that will manage the behaviour of the whole formation.

It is a Brazilian Army programme to develop a drone swarm system that lets a single operator coordinate multiple SD10 quadcopters from a ground station.

The project involves 30 SD10 quadcopters: five Top units, 15 Regular units and ten Simplified units, with different cameras, batteries and lidar anti-collision features.

SkyDrones designed and integrated the aircraft, while IME's LIARC laboratory is responsible for the artificial intelligence, coordination algorithms and integrated control software.

The SD10 is a quadcopter with a maximum take-off weight of 10 kg, IP54 protection, a maximum speed of 54 km/h, a cruise speed of 36 km/h, a service ceiling of 3,000 metres and wind tolerance up to 8 m/s.

It must show that the algorithms can safely and reliably manage all 30 aircraft flying simultaneously; the transition to a military capability will depend on test results and on incorporating technologies more resistant to electronic warfare.

He was a colonel regarded as the patron of the Military Engineering Corps, and the drone swarm project is named after him.

The Top and Regular versions also include a rotating lidar for 360-degree anti-collision detection, a feature that is not present in the Simplified configuration.

One of the relevant aspects of the project is the open architecture of its control systems. The SD10 uses customised versions of ArduPilot and PX4 as the basis for its autopilot, with communication through the MAVLink protocol. Access to the code and to the software development kit (SDK) will allow IME researchers to modify and integrate the coordination algorithms without depending on closed proprietary solutions.

For navigation, the system combines dual-antenna GNSS satellite positioning with RTK correction, inertial units, barometers and compasses. It also incorporates optical flow sensors and altitude lidar which, according to the specifications released by SkyDrones, make it possible to hold position without GPS assistance at heights of up to 30 metres.

The project is named after Colonel Ricardo Franco de Almeida Serra, regarded as the patron of the Military Engineering Corps. Beyond the delivery of the drones, its importance lies in giving the Army a platform to research autonomous operation technologies, coordination between aircraft and resilience against electronic interference.

In that sense, the programme still has to demonstrate that the algorithms can safely and reliably manage all 30 aircraft flying simultaneously. The transition from an experimental prototype to a military capability will depend on the results of those tests and on the possibility of subsequently incorporating technologies that are more resistant to electronic warfare.
